questions.question: Write a four-organism food chain from a South African ecosystem, state what the arrows represent, and give the trophic level (name and number) of each organism.
questions.expected_answer: E.g. phytoplankton → zooplankton → sardine → Cape gannet (or grass → locust → lizard → eagle). Arrows show the direction of energy flow ('is eaten by'). Phytoplankton: producer, first trophic level; zooplankton: primary consumer, second; sardine: secondary consumer, third; gannet: tertiary consumer, fourth.

questions.question: In a savanna food web, jackals eat locusts and rodents, and eagles eat lizards and snakes; lizards eat locusts; locusts eat grass. Predict and explain two effects of removing all the jackals.
questions.expected_answer: Fewer jackals means fewer locusts and rodents are eaten, so their populations increase; more locusts eat more grass, so grass decreases and grazers have less food; lizards may increase with more locusts, so eagles may have more prey. Each step follows an arrow in the web, and the web shows how one change spreads through interdependent populations.

questions.question: Grass in a field stores 10 000 kJ of energy. Using the ten percent rule, calculate the energy stored at the next three trophic levels, name the four ways energy is lost between levels, and explain why food chains rarely exceed four or five links.
questions.expected_answer: Primary consumers 1000 kJ; secondary consumers 100 kJ; tertiary consumers 10 kJ. Losses: parts not eaten (roots, bones); parts not digested (dung); energy used in respiration and released as heat (the largest loss); other waste such as urine. Only energy built into new tissue passes on, so after four or five transfers too little remains to support a population; the levels form a pyramid of energy.
